readerTitle: Why some deadlines help customers decide and others make them leave
caseNote: 일상 관찰 (늘 붙어 있는 '마감 임박' 안내문) + 가상 사례 (B2B 회계 서비스, 회사 안의 운영팀)
insight: 정직한 긴급함은 판매자의 마감이 아니라 고객이 기다릴 때 치르는 실제 비용과 실제 기한에서 나온다.
misconception: 긴급함은 곧 압박 기술이다. 그래서 가짜 마감을 만들거나, 정직한 판매자라면 긴급함을 아예 말하지 말아야 한다.

sources.text: 영업에서 널리 쓰이는 원칙 (지연 비용, 고객 쪽 기한 중심의 의사결정 지원)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 특정 연구나 통계는 인용하지 않았습니다. 첫 카드의 '늘 붙어 있는 마감 안내문'은 흔한 관찰로만 서술했습니다.
가상 수치 확인: 회계 서비스 온보딩 6주, 연말 결산까지 8주 → 2주 안에 시작해야 함. 운영팀 사례: 수작업 월 30시간, 성수기까지 2개월, 도입·교육 6주 → 지금 시작해야 성수기 전에 준비됨.

cards.title: The sign that says "Offer ends Friday" every Friday
body: You've probably walked past one. A shop window or a website banner promises the deal ends this week. Next week, the same sign is still there.
The first time, it works. The second time, you learn to ignore it. Some urgency moves people. Some just teaches them to wait.

image.label: Shop window sign reading Offer ends Friday, with a calendar showing many Fridays
image.brief: 가게 진열창에 'Offer ends Friday!' 안내문. 옆 벽 달력에는 여러 주의 금요일마다 같은 안내문 그림이 반복되어 있고, 지나가는 사람이 무심하게 고개를 돌림. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The client keeps saying "soon."
body: You run a bookkeeping firm. A restaurant group likes your proposal but hasn't signed in a month. You know two things: setting up a new client takes about six weeks, and their year-end close is eight weeks away.

options.text: A 15% discount if they sign by Friday
options.feedback: It may get a signature, but the deadline is yours, not theirs. You give away margin and teach them your prices bend under delay.

options.text: A simple timeline: to be ready for year-end, setup must start within two weeks
options.feedback: You add no pressure of your own. You show a deadline they already have, and what waiting will cost them.

options.text: A friendly check-in every week until they're ready
options.feedback: Polite and low-risk, but it gives them no reason to decide now. They may realise the timing problem only after it's too late.

cards.title: The calendar did the selling.
body: The owner sent a one-page timeline. Six weeks of setup. Year-end close in eight. The gap was two weeks.
The client's finance lead had not done that math. She signed the next week, at full price.
Nothing about the offer changed. What changed was that the client could now see a cost of waiting that had been there all along.

image.label: Timeline showing six weeks of setup ending just before year-end close
image.brief: 가로 타임라인. 'Today'에서 시작하는 6주짜리 'Setup' 막대, 8주 지점에 'Year-end close' 깃발. 그 사이 2주 틈을 노란색으로 강조하고 'Start by here' 라벨.

cards.title: Honest urgency
body: **Honest urgency** is a reason to decide now that is true and belongs to the customer. It comes from their deadlines, their cost of delay or a real limit, not from your sales target.
A simple test: would this reason still be true if you didn't need the sale this month? If yes, saying it out loud is helping. If no, it's pressure.

cards.title: Where real urgency comes from
body: Look for urgency in three places before you invent any.
list: **The customer's own deadline:** a season, an audit, a launch, a contract ending
**The cost of waiting:** hours, money or customers lost each month nothing changes
**A real limit on your side:** booked-up capacity, or a price change already announced to everyone
cards.callout: Your job is to make the clock visible, not to build a new one.
cards.softwareNote: An end-of-quarter discount is the seller's deadline. A stronger reason is the customer's: their old vendor's contract renews in 60 days, and moving their data takes 45.

cards.title: A fake deadline works once.
body: When a deadline passes and the offer quietly returns, customers learn something. Your deadlines are negotiable. Next time, the smart move is to wait.
The same goes for inside a company. A manager who calls every request "urgent" soon finds that nothing they send gets read first.
Honest urgency gets stronger with use, because each time you're proven right.

cards.title: Sometimes the honest answer is "no rush."
body: Don't inflate the cost of delay. If you stretch the numbers, the customer will check them, and you lose both the deal and the trust.

And if there's no real reason to act now, say so. "Nothing changes if you wait a month" can build more trust than any offer. It also tells you the real objection may be something else, which is the subject of handling "Not right now."

cards.title: Now you're selling inside your own company.
body: You lead an operations team. You want the finance director to approve a scheduling tool. Your team spends about 30 hours a month doing it by hand. Busy season starts in two months, and setup plus training takes six weeks.
The director says: "Let's revisit next quarter."

options.text: Say other teams are about to claim the budget
options.feedback: If it isn't confirmed, it's pressure dressed as news. If the director checks, your next request gets less trust.

options.text: Show that next quarter means busy season without the tool, plus the hours lost until then
options.feedback: You use their calendar and real costs. The director can still say no, but now it's an informed no.

options.text: Agree, and ask what would need to be true to approve it
options.feedback: Good for learning the real objection, but the director still doesn't see that waiting has a cost.

cards.title: Show the clock that's already ticking.
body: The best reason to decide now is one the customer already has but hasn't seen yet.

**Try it today:** pick one stalled deal or request. Write down the customer's real deadline and what one month of waiting costs them. If you can't find either, stop pushing and ask what's really holding it up.
